notes.meaning: News spread quickly throughout Judea that non-Jewish people had accepted God's message. This was startling to many Jewish believers because Gentiles had long been viewed as outsiders to God's covenant promises. The apostles and local believers were eager to learn how this sudden change had taken place.

When Peter returned to Jerusalem, Jewish believers sharply challenged his conduct. Their complaint was not about his preaching, but that he had entered a Gentile home and shared a meal with uncircumcised men, which broke traditional Jewish rules of separation. They were alarmed that he seemed to set aside centuries of sacred custom.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The Catholic Church teaches that Peter held supreme authority as the visible head of the universal church, even while answering questions from fellow believers.

notes.meaning: Peter did not take offense or pull rank as an apostle, but calmly shared the entire story in order. He knew that an honest, step-by-step account of what had happened was the best way to clear away misunderstanding. By explaining every event as it occurred, he showed that he was simply following God's lead.

Peter explained that while praying in the coastal town of Joppa, God gave him a vision that paused his normal physical senses. He saw a large sheet lowered straight from heaven by its four corners, coming right down to him. When he looked inside, he saw all kinds of animals, wild beasts, reptiles, and birds.

A heavenly voice told Peter to stand up, kill, and eat. Peter refused immediately, explaining that he had strictly kept Jewish food laws his entire life and had never let anything unclean touch his lips. Even when hungry, he was determined to remain faithful to what he had always believed God required.

The voice answered from heaven a second time, telling Peter not to call unclean what God Himself has made clean. This exchange was repeated three times so Peter could have no doubt about the message. After that, the entire sheet with all the creatures was pulled back up into heaven.

At that very moment, three messengers arrived at the house where Peter was staying, having been sent from Caesarea. The exact timing showed that the vision was not a random dream, but God's way of preparing Peter for these unexpected visitors.

The Holy Spirit told Peter to go with the messengers without doubting or making any difference between Jews and Gentiles. Wisely anticipating that questions would be asked later, Peter took six Jewish Christian brothers along with him as companions and eyewitnesses. Together, all seven entered the Gentile home.

Cornelius told them that an angel had stood in his house and ordered him to send to Joppa for Peter. The angel explained that Peter would bring the message of the gospel, through which Cornelius and his entire family would be saved. Salvation means being rescued from the guilt and penalty of sin to receive eternal life with God.

Right as Peter began his message, the Holy Spirit came down on these Gentile listeners with the very same power experienced by the Jewish disciples on Pentecost. God did not wait for a ritual or human approval before giving His Spirit. This visible gift showed beyond doubt that God fully accepted them.

Seeing this happen reminded Peter of what Jesus had promised before His ascension, that while John baptized with water, His followers would be baptized with the Holy Spirit. Peter realized that this promise was not meant only for Jews, but for anyone who believes. The spiritual cleansing given by Christ is what truly counts.

Peter reasoned that since God gave these Gentiles the exact same gift He gave the apostles when they believed in Jesus, no human being had the right to stand in God's way. He was merely God's instrument, not the judge of who could receive grace. Welcoming them in baptism and fellowship was simply obeying what God had already done.

Hearing Peter's evidence silenced the critics and moved them to praise God. They celebrated the amazing news that God had granted Gentiles repentance unto life, which means turning from sin and false beliefs to receive everlasting life. God's clear working had overcome their long-held prejudices.

The story now turns back to the believers who had fled Jerusalem during the wave of persecution that began after Stephen was killed. As they traveled north along the coast to Phoenicia, across to Cyprus, and over to Antioch, they shared the good news, but only with other Jews. They still did not realize that the gospel was intended for everyone.

A few of these scattered believers, originally from the island of Cyprus and the African city of Cyrene, took a bold new step when they reached Antioch. They began preaching the good news about the Lord Jesus directly to Greek Gentiles. This marked the very first open mission to non-Jewish people.

The hand of the Lord was with these preachers, meaning God's divine power worked directly through their message. Because God empowered their words, a large number of people believed the gospel and turned from their old idolatry to serve the true Lord. Human preaching only changes lives when God's power accompanies it.

When reports of this great revival reached the church in Jerusalem, the leaders chose Barnabas to travel to Antioch to see what was happening. Barnabas was an ideal messenger because he was known for his generous spirit and had family roots in Cyprus like several of the preachers. Jerusalem wanted to support and guide this new work rather than shut it down.

When Barnabas arrived and saw the clear evidence of God's grace in the transformed lives of the converts, he was overjoyed. Living up to his name as an encourager, he urged everyone to remain steadfast and cling to the Lord with all their heart. He knew that genuine faith needs steady resolve when trials come.

differ.view: God gives the grace, but believers must use it and keep holding on. Someone who stops clinging to the Lord can fall from grace and lose salvation.

notes.meaning: Barnabas was a good man, guided by the Holy Spirit and filled with strong faith in God. Because he was humble and lacked jealousy, his ministry bore rich fruit, and even more people were brought to faith in the Lord. His gracious character helped the young church flourish.

Realizing the work was too big for one person, Barnabas traveled to Tarsus to find Saul and bring him back to Antioch. For an entire year, the two men gathered with the church and taught large crowds of new believers. It was here in Antioch that the disciples were first called Christians, a name pointing out that their lives were centered on Christ.

During that productive year, some Christian prophets traveled down from the mother church in Jerusalem to Antioch. These were teachers gifted by the Holy Spirit to strengthen believers and, at special times, reveal what was coming in the future. Their arrival showed the close bond between the two churches.

One of these prophets, named Agabus, was prompted by the Holy Spirit to stand up and announce that a widespread famine would strike the Roman world. Luke points out that this severe food shortage happened just as predicted during the reign of Emperor Claudius. God gave the church advance warning so they could get ready.

The believers in Antioch decided to gather financial relief for the Christians in Judea, with each person giving according to their means. They sent their gift to the church elders in Jerusalem by Barnabas and Saul. This generous support gave living proof that Gentile and Jewish believers were truly united in one loving spiritual family.
